newsitem.title: UK: British premier's wife called in to help campaign.
newsitem.headline: British premier's wife called in to help campaign.

text.p: Tax cuts and falling unemployment have not helped John Major in the polls, nor have attacks on his Labour opponents as red-eyed demons. So now the British prime minister is wheeling out a new secret weapon -- his wife Norma.

With eight months at most before the next general election, managers of Major's ruling Conservative party have persuaded Norma to step out of the shadows and accompany her husband on a high-profile two-week campaign swing starting on Wednesday.
It is the first time she has gone on such a tour, which kicks off with a speech to businessmen to Glasgow.

Unassuming, housewifely and evidently sweet-natured, according to an admiring Daily Telegraph editorial, Norma Major is the antithesis of hard-nosed U.S. political wives such as Hillary Clinton and Elizabeth Dole.
And that is precisely the point in the eyes of Conservative strategists struggling to claw back the opposition Labour party's 20-percentage-point lead in recent public opinion polls.
They see her homely, sympathetic image as a decided vote winner -- in unspoken contrast to Cherie Booth, the assertive high-flying lawyer married to Labour leader Tony Blair.

"She's a super lady, greatly loved in the Tory party, has been by his side over the years. I am encouraged by the fact that many...are now recognising that fact," Conservative party chairman Brian Mawhinney told BBC radio.
"She has been so supportive of the prime minister and will continue to be so, I can assure you of that," he added.
Supportive yes, but sometimes against her will.
Standing on the steps of 10 Downing St, the prime minister's London residence, when her husband succeeded Margaret Thatcher in 1990, she looked like a rabbit trapped in car headlights.
"I did not regard it as a particularly joyous occasion. I took several months really to sort it out. Things were happening to me that I wasn't prepared for," she said later.
Fiercely protective of her children's privacy, she refused for a long time to move to Downing St from the family home in Huntingdon, eastern England.
Opera-loving Norma also made a point of pursuing her own interests, including writing an authoritative biography of Australian soprano Dame Joan Sutherland.
She played a part in the 1992 election campaign but often looked ill at ease as her husband mounted soapboxes to urge electors to vote Conservative.

Although Britain's first lady now is happy to return to the public gaze, Conservative officials said there was no question of her trying to emulate Hillary Clinton by taking on a public speaking role.
And that, commentators agree, is smart politics.

"What might well be going through Tory minds is the thought that by projecting Norma Major as a quiet, loyal but in her own terms successful person, they can give something of a boost to John Major's own personal image," political pollster Peter Kellner said.
